questions.enonce_markdown:
3. (a) (i) Briefly explain how Logic and History are related:

(ii) Define the Cognitive use of Language. (2 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Logic and History.** History studies past events and tries to establish what really happened from evidence (documents, testimonies, remains). Logic is the **tool** of the historian: the historian must reason correctly from sources to conclusions, weigh evidence, avoid fallacies (such as false cause or hasty generalisation) and test whether an interpretation follows from the facts. In return, the history of Logic shows how the science itself developed (Aristotle, the medieval logicians, modern symbolic logic). So history supplies the facts and logic supplies the correct way of reasoning about them.

**(ii) The cognitive use of language** is the use of language to **convey information**: to state facts, describe, report, affirm or deny something, or to give reasons for a claim. Cognitive statements are **true or false**, so they can be the premises or conclusion of an argument. Example: "Yaoundé is the capital of Cameroon." (It differs from the emotive use, which expresses or arouses feelings, and from the directive use, which commands or requests.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Distinguish between the following:

(i) The Invertend and the Inverse:

(ii) State two General Rules of the Standard Form Categorical Syllogism according to Distribution of Terms: (2 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** In **inversion** we infer from a proposition another proposition whose subject is the **contradictory of the original subject**. The **invertend** is the original proposition; the **inverse** is the proposition obtained. Inversion is valid only for A and E propositions:
- invertend A: "All S are P"; inverse: "Some non-S are not P" (O);
- invertend E: "No S is P"; inverse: "Some non-S are P" (I).

Example: invertend "All teachers are graduates"; inverse "Some non-teachers are not graduates".

**(ii) Rules of distribution** (any two):
1. The **middle term must be distributed at least once** in the premises (otherwise: fallacy of undistributed middle).
2. A term that is **distributed in the conclusion must be distributed in the premise** where it appears (otherwise: illicit major if it is the major term, illicit minor if it is the minor term).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) (i) When is a Dilemma considered to be Destructive?

(ii) State the rules of Hypothetical Syllogism: (2 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** A dilemma is **destructive** when its disjunctive premise **denies the consequents** of the conditional premises, so that the conclusion **denies the antecedents** (either one or the other). Form: If A then B; if C then D; either not-B or not-D; therefore either not-A or not-C. (In a **constructive** dilemma the disjunctive premise affirms the antecedents and the conclusion affirms the consequents.) Example: "If he were honest, he would return the money; if he were wise, he would not hide it; either he did not return it or he hid it; therefore either he is not honest or he is not wise."

**(ii) Rules of the (mixed) hypothetical syllogism**, whose major premise is conditional ("If A then B"):
1. If the minor premise **affirms the antecedent**, the conclusion affirms the consequent (modus ponens: valid).
2. If the minor premise **denies the consequent**, the conclusion denies the antecedent (modus tollens: valid).
3. Affirming the consequent is invalid (fallacy of the consequent).
4. Denying the antecedent is invalid (fallacy of the antecedent).

For the **pure** hypothetical syllogism: the consequent of the first premise must be the antecedent of the second, and the conclusion joins the antecedent of the first premise to the consequent of the second.

(e) (i) State the rule of Conjunction:

(ii) What are the Logical Constants for the Wedge and the Triple Bar? (2 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Rule of conjunction.** A conjunction $p \cdot q$ is **true only when both conjuncts are true**; it is false when at least one conjunct is false (that is, in the three rows TF, FT and FF). As a rule of inference: from $p$ and from $q$ asserted separately we may infer $p \cdot q$.

| $p$ | $q$ | $p \cdot q$ |
|---|---|---|
| T | T | T |
| T | F | F |
| F | T | F |
| F | F | F |

**(ii) Logical constants.** The **wedge** $\vee$ stands for **disjunction**, "or" (inclusive: "p or q or both"). The **triple bar** $\equiv$ stands for **equivalence** (material equivalence), "if and only if" ("p is equivalent to q"): true when $p$ and $q$ have the same truth-value.
